Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For a civilian assault trauma, 'talks about military' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the assault specifically involved military context, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It is not supported by the other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'I feel guilty for surviving when others did not' implies a trauma involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty context. That does not cohere with the rest of this profile, which otherwise describes an individual assault without any indication that others were killed.

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: This appraisal is the main incoherent item in the profile. The rest of the report is organized around fear, betrayal, hypervigilance, male-related/interpersonal triggers, and fragmented sensory trauma memory after assault. In contrast, fearing that she will lose control of her own rage and do something terrible introduces a perpetration/anger-control theme that is not supported by the triggers, threat items, or memory content. It does not fit the dominant cognitive formulation in which negative appraisals feed threat and memory; the other appraisal items plausibly amplify fear and mistrust, but this one points to a different clinical concern not otherwise represented in the profile. Given the otherwise tightly fear-based assault presentation, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the selected set.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: This threat item is the least coherent element in the profile. The rest of the selected triggers, appraisals, and memory items consistently describe an interpersonal assault formulation centered on men, betrayal, mistrust, conversational/emotional triggers, and trauma memories. By contrast, needing to stay alert at night implies a more generalized ongoing danger-monitoring pattern that is not specifically supported by the selected triggers or appraisals. It is not impossible in PTSD, but here it fits less well than the other threat items and is weakly linked to the formulation, especially because Threat has no active edge to Maladaptive Strategies and the profile lacks other nighttime/sleep-related material.

vignette: Maria, a 54‑year‑old European chef, had spent two decades mastering the rhythms of her kitchen, moving between prep tables and ovens with a confidence that felt almost automatic. One November evening, as she plated a special truffle risotto for a private dinner, a patron—a middle‑aged man with a nervous laugh—moved too close to the serving counter. He began to press his hand against her thigh, insisting on a touch that Maria quickly pushed away. When he pushed back, the contact turned forceful, and the man shoved her so hard that she fell against the stainless steel counter, her body mirroring the assault’s sudden, violent position. The night ended with a silent, wordless realization that the event was more than a mere altercation; it was a betrayal of the trust she had placed in a stranger who had come in as a customer. In the days that followed, Maria could not find the words to describe what had happened. Her memories of the night arrived as fragmented, disjointed images that refused to fit together. When a friend asked about her night, Maria’s mind flicked to the assault, her body instinctively shuddering to the same tense posture she had held when shoved. These bodily reenactments occurred even as she talked about nothing related to the kitchen. The nonverbal, disjointed nature of her recall fed into her growing sense of betrayal: the man who had been a customer had become a threat. The feeling that she could never know who might harm her grew stronger, and she began to mistrust anyone who entered her space, especially when they were male. Her fear of harm, once a vague worry, became a concrete belief that strangers were potential threats, and this belief led her to see movement—an unexpected shift in a staff member’s position—as a danger, setting off a startle response that left her breathing heavy and eyes wide. The triggers that Maria identified were, therefore, more than mere conversation topics. When her husband or a colleague spoke of a recent romantic breakup, the words seemed to echo the intimacy that had been violated. In the moments of “emotional closeness” that she once enjoyed sharing recipes and kitchen jokes, Maria felt her heart race as if a threat lurked just beyond the doorway. The presence of men alone in the kitchen—her sous‑chef, a delivery driver, a cleaning crew—prompted a hyperalert state; she found herself watching every movement as if anticipating a sudden push. Each of these triggers not only dredged up memories of the assault, complete with the bodily position she had endured, but also reinforced her negative appraisals. She felt that those topics, those closeness, those male presences, were reminders that she could be betrayed again, which in turn sharpened her sense that strangers were dangerous and that the world was a place where harm was inevitable. Maria’s negative appraisals fed back into her perception of threat. The belief that anyone could strike her made ordinary movements feel menacing, and the startle reactions she experienced became a constant backdrop to her life. When a coworker asked her to walk a crate of produce down a hallway, Maria felt the urge to freeze, as if she were on a silent edge of a cliff. Each time she felt threatened, she recalled the assault, the bodily reenactment of her body bent and tense, and the sense that the event had not been an isolated occurrence. That memory, in turn, reinforced her mistrust of strangers and heightened her fear that someone might once again violate her, turning the triggers she dreaded into a self‑fulfilling loop of anxiety. The sense that being alone with men in the kitchen was a trigger became more pronounced as her belief that the world was dangerous grew. At work, Maria’s sense of threat and betrayal altered her routine. She began to avoid tasks that required prolonged interaction with male staff. When a sous‑chef asked her to adjust a dish, she would look around, waiting for any sudden movement. She no longer smiled at the same jovial banter that once lightened the kitchen’s atmosphere. The shift in her behavior not only strained her relationships with colleagues but also caused her to miss critical prep times, as she hesitated to step into areas where she felt the threat of a sudden push. The occupational demands of her trade—quick decisions, precise timing, teamwork—now clashed with her internal alarm system that saw every gesture as a potential threat. Maria’s decision to seek help came after a week of almost being unable to enter the kitchen. She had a scheduled dinner service that night, and the thought of standing in the middle of a bustling kitchen filled her with a terror that made her feel physically ill. She feared that the startle she would experience would prevent her from completing the service, and more importantly, she feared that it would bring back the assault’s memory so vividly that she would collapse. Her most urgent hope is to regain the ability to function in her professional environment without the looming sense of threat, while her greatest fear remains the possibility that the trigger—an unexpected movement, a close conversation, a male presence—will unspool her past again, forcing her back into that unsafe, betrayed space.
